Different choirs change the timbre: plucking close to the nut emphasises the higher overtones and gives a nasal quality. Early instruments were smaller and higher in pitch; later ones used more choirs and two keyboards to widen the choice of pitch; compared with the small plucked keyboard instruments of the same family, the harpsichord is usually larger and can have several choirs and stops.

The harpsichord is a European plucked keyboard instrument, Hornbostel-Sachs number 314.122-6-8. Pressing a key raises a wooden plectrum, which plucks a string stretched over the soundboard; the body is a wooden case, often with several choirs of strings, with levers or two keyboards to choose timbre and volume. With the virginal, muselaar and spinet it belongs to the plucked keyboard family, and in the Renaissance and Baroque it was used for solos, accompaniment and continuo groups; after the twentieth century it appears in historical performance, new works and some popular music.
大鍵琴琴身以木製琴箱構成，音板為薄木片，常見雲杉、冷杉，部分義大利琴用柏木。十六: The body of the harpsichord is a wooden case, and the soundboard is a thin sheet of wood, commonly spruce or fir, with some Italian instruments using cypress. Sixteenth-century Italian designs used low-tension brass strings, while Flemish designs used high-tension steel strings in the treble. The plucking part is a wooden jack carrying a quill, a leather or a modern plastic plectrum. The nut, bridge and wrest plank are hardwood, the bridge has metal string pins, and the damping cloth and the jack rail are covered with felt.
大鍵琴約於十四世紀末出現，早期體積小、音高較高。十六世紀義大利形成輕薄琴殼、低張: The harpsichord appeared around the end of the fourteenth century, small and high in pitch at first. In sixteenth-century Italy a tradition formed of light, thin cases, low-tension brass strings, a single keyboard and two choirs of strings; the southern Netherlands took a different path, with heavier construction, high-tension steel strings and two keyboards. In the Renaissance and Baroque it was widely used for accompaniment and solo playing, and in the Baroque it was a standard member of the continuo. In the eighteenth century its form spread to France, England and Germany, and different choirs and stops increased its expressiveness. After the piano appeared around 1700 the harpsichord was gradually replaced by the end of the eighteenth century, surviving in the nineteenth only in opera recitative; in the twentieth it was revived through historical performance and historical instrument making.

A beginner can first practise pressing and releasing a single key to confirm the order of sounding and damping, then use the selector to switch between choirs and change volume and timbre.
